name: PT Perusahaan Perkebunan London Sumatra Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: London Sumatra — an estate the market barely pays for
frontmatter.summary: A mature planter whose cash is most of its market value, and whose estate the market barely pays for. We stay BUY at Rp4,689 (206.8%). GAPKI's warning that El Nino could cost Indonesian output up to 3m tonnes in the 2027 harvest is a national, industry-wide loss that changes no base input because it is not company guidance, but it hardens both the bear's volume shock and the bull's price squeeze [S24, F68].
thesis: Cash of IDR8,516.3bn and no interest-bearing debt at 30 September 2026 is most of the IDR10,639.1bn market capitalisation [S8, F37].
A mature estate earned 43.5% EBITDA margins at the deck price, with most output sold domestically to the parent at a persistent discount to the export benchmark [S7, S15].
The dividend is covered at a thirty per cent payout and a IDR750.0bn buyback is running; a probability-weighted part of the buyback is in the target and the dividend step-up is not [S12, S9].
The DCF, the config-blend multiples and book value all sit far above the price; the reverse DCF implies CPO near US$640/t [S0].
The risk is structural: related-party offtake, a controlling holder with no obligation to distribute, and a payout already cut once [S7, S12, S13].

catalysts.event: Implementing finance-ministry regulation for the DHE SDA conversion amendment; no direct effect on LSIP, watched only for the exchange-rate channel

The DSI single export channel is due to go live for coal, CPO and ferro alloy (reported, unconfirmed pending the implementing rule); the published intermediary fee and the parent's export netback are the watch items
Buyback window closes; B50 biodiesel mandate and the monthly CPO export levy reset
FY2026 audited results and the final dividend declaration for the year
First-half production and the El Nino impact on FFB yields; GAPKI dates the heaviest 2027-harvest loss to this window

blocks.text: **Update, 12 November 2026 — the El Nino warning.** At GAPKI's Bali conference, chairman Eddy Martono said El Nino could cost Indonesian palm output up to 3m tonnes in the 2027 harvest [S24, F68, S22]. No model input changes: the loss is national, not company guidance, and London Sumatra's nine-month CPO sales were ahead of the prior year [S3, F47], so volume stays at 300 kt [S0]. It hardens the tails — the bear's volume shortfall and the bull's price squeeze from a supply loss meeting 14m tonnes of B50 demand [S24, S22]. The price is Rp1,560 on 12 November 2026 [S0].

The DSI export channel is reported, not regulated. Press reports put coal, CPO and ferro alloy through Danantara's portal from 1 January 2027 [S20], but no rule is in our archive. London Sumatra sells oil palm and seed domestically; its IDR43.7bn export line is rubber, cocoa and tea [S7, F49], so the regime reaches it only through the parent's refining netback, carried in the bear [S21].

At Rp1,560 the company is worth about IDR10,639.1bn, against IDR8,516.3bn of cash and no interest-bearing debt [S8]: the market pays barely more than the cash pile for the estate and mills. Yet the estate earned 43.5% EBITDA margins, IDR1,887.8bn of net profit and Rp277 per share in the last audited year [S7], and nine-month profit rose two fifths [S3, S8]. Our target is Rp4,689, 206.8% above the price: a DCF at the through-cycle deck plus cash with a probability-weighted governance discount on the related-party slice, corroborated by two multiples. The reverse DCF is the discipline: the price implies CPO of US$640/t against a deck of 1,240.0 USD/t [S0, S15] — either the deck is wrong or the cash never reaches shareholders.

PT Perusahaan Perkebunan London Sumatra Indonesia Tbk has nucleus estates in North Sumatra, South Sumatra, East Kalimantan, Java and Sulawesi [S6]. It sold 290.0 kt CPO of CPO from just over one hundred and ten thousand planted hectares — about ninety-one thousand oil palm, sixteen thousand rubber and the balance cocoa and tea — and manages about thirty-five thousand hectares of plasma estates [S6]. Oil palm products dominate revenue; SumBio seeds and a small rubber, cocoa and tea residual are the rest, and there is no refining of consequence — this is an upstream grower and miller whose economics are the CPO price less the cost of a tonne [S7].

More than three fifths of revenue is sold to PT Salim Ivomas Pratama, the listed subsidiary of Indofood Agri Resources that controls London Sumatra; almost two thirds moves within the group and only a sliver is exported [S7]. Sales are market-referenced, and the audited realisation was stable in rupiah against the domestic Harga Referensi/KPB; the 2026 dollar ratio is measured against a benchmark the World Bank replaced in January 2026 and is not comparable with the audited years [S7, S15, F41]. Strategy is replanting, yield recovery and cost control: planted area has drifted down over five years and there is no announced expansion or downstream project [S6].

The Salim family controls the company through Salim Ivomas and Indofood Agri Resources: PT Salim Ivomas Pratama holds 59.5% and Indofood Agri a further small stake, so the group controls just under three fifths and the public holds 40.4% [S13]. All 6,820 m shares are listed; no special-monitoring-board designation or notation letter appears in the filings we hold [S7, S8]. That ownership explains both the stable offtake and the persistent discount.

Indonesia is the world's largest CPO producer, and the price London Sumatra receives is set globally. The deck has CPO averaging 1,135.0 USD/t this year, rising next year and easing toward a long-run anchor of 1,150.0 USD/t in FY2029 money escalated with Indonesian inflation [S0, S15].

On 12 November GAPKI put a number on the weather. Its chairman said El Nino could cost Indonesian production up to 3m tonnes, heaviest in the 2027 harvest, after smallholders deferred fertiliser and fires damaged estates [S24, F68, S22]. Against that, the B50 mandate that began on 1 July 2026 needs 14m tonnes of CPO a year [S22], so the domestic balance tightens. The tonnage is an industry forecast, not company guidance, and the same shock the deck's premium embeds [S24].

Policy is active. Indonesia taxes CPO exports through a levy plus duty that moves monthly with a reference price; for November the combined charge fell by a fifth to 246.4 USD/t per tonne, borne by the exporter and relevant here only at the margin because sales are domestic [S10]. The move from forty to fifty per cent biodiesel is the largest source of incremental domestic demand [S10]. The exchange-control change is separate: PP 21/2026 brings DHE SDA onshore for twelve months with rupiah conversion capped at half, and implementing rules are due by end-November [S17, S16]; it changes the currency of the onshore balance, not dollars received, and is negligible because palm and seed revenue is rupiah revenue from a domestic customer [S7]. Export logistics are being centralised: from 1 January 2027 coal, CPO and ferro alloy would file through DSI's portal on reports we treat as unconfirmed [S20]. No fee is published, so the incidence is indirect — the parent's export netback — and the bear carries a sized pass-through [S21].

No domestic levy is in force in November 2026; the levy and duty are export charges [S10]. But B50 has a funding need, and the one policy that could meet it from a seller like London Sumatra is a charge on domestic sales, so we price a levy of thirty to sixty dollars per tonne in the bear. Competition is a cost-curve story: peers compete on yield, age profile and mill distance, not brand. London Sumatra's estates are old; its cash cost of 7,791,431 rupiah per tonne rose because external FFB purchases climbed by more than a third [S7, S6]. The moat is land and logistics — HGU rights, mills, plasma partnerships and the parent's refining system — real barriers that do not protect margins from a falling price [S6]. Five forces are unfavourable on the customer side, neutral on suppliers and favourable against new entrants [S6].

The data pack misstates the last audited year. Revenue rose 20.8% to IDR5,511.7bn on higher CPO volume and price; operating profit was IDR2,008.4bn and net profit to the parent IDR1,887.8bn [S7]. The pack's depreciation is unusable — a few billion against audited IDR389.5bn — so we key the audited figure, lift FY2025 EBITDA to IDR2,397.8bn and margin to 43.5%, restate FY2024 the same way, and strike multiples off this base [S7, F12].

The cash cost is 7,791,431 rupiah per tonne, backed out of audited cost of sales after removing depreciation and allocating other costs; it rose because external FFB purchases climbed more than a third, and we hold it in real terms with inflation [S7]. Realisation is calibrated on nine-month interim: CPO revenue over CPO volume gives a dollar price flat against prior year while the benchmark rose, ratio 75.8% [S8, S3, S0]. The World Bank replaced its palm-oil series from January 2026, and pre-2026 averages and the 2026 monthly tape are not homogeneous [S15, S0]. Audited 858.1 USD/t against 1,007.0 USD/t is not like-for-like; the domestic series is homogeneous and LSIP invoices against the Harga Referensi, averaging 14,234 rupiah per kilogram [S10, F41].

Revenue rises to IDR5,988.9bn this year, EBITDA IDR2,684.3bn, net profit IDR2,189.5bn and Rp321 per share; margin peaks with deck and compresses as price eases. Volume held at 300 kt, a shade below nine‑month plus normal Q4, because estate mature, planted area drifted down and GAPKI warning national, not guidance [S0, S7, S3, S24]. On the like-for-like comparison the model's dollar ASP of 860.3 USD/t at the current-year benchmark is flat against last year's realised 858.1 USD/t [S8, S3, S15].

Capex runs at 7.9% of revenue, working capital small; EBITDA becomes cash [S7]: IDR8,516.3bn at third quarter against zero interest-bearing debt [S8]. Forecast holds working capital at FY2025 ratio; the bear stretches it to the FY2024 spike; capex escalates with inflation, depreciation from the audited note [S0, F34, S7, F13, S8]. Dividend Rp83 at thirty per cent payout, buyback further return [S12, S9]. Operating cash flow of IDR3,015.7bn exceeded net profit and the accruals ratio is negative three years [S7, S0]. Inventories up to IDR830.8bn, a build of a third against a tenth of revenue growth that one quarter explains but a second would not [S8, S3].

We use a DCF as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and P/BV cross-checks at sixty, twenty-five and fifteen per cent — the method set for a price-taking grower whose value is the cash a mature asset earns over a cycle. Terminal growth is 2.5%, long-run rupiah inflation [S0].

The cost of equity is 11.2%: the rupiah ten-year yield 7.4% [S18], beta 0.80 times the mature premium 4.2% plus country premium 2.5%, net of the 1.6% sovereign spread [S19]; with no net debt WACC equals it.

The DCF gives Rp5,044 per share, a terminal value of 45.8% of it, on an enterprise value of IDR24,713.7bn plus September net cash and the associate. The anchor is the deck's through-cycle 1,150.0 USD/t in FY2029 money escalated with inflation, so the first terminal year is 1,178.8 USD/t, not the 1,180.0 USD/t print [S0, S15]. We use the deck's shape, not a cross-series level: the World Bank replaced its palm-oil series in January 2026 [S15 p.3], so pre-2026 averages and the old FY2023 trough are not homogeneous and we quote no level from them. On the new series the anchor is about two and a half per cent below spot and about one and a third per cent above the 1,135.0 USD/t deck average. Running the DCF at spot leaves the value within a tenth of the base.

The IDR1,261.1bn associate line is four equity-method holdings — Asian Assets Management in Singapore and PT Aston Inti Makmur in Jakarta, each roughly a quarter held, plus two smaller industrial-timber holdings [S7, S8, F62]. Both larger holdings are private and carried below attributable net assets; the nine-month share of associate profit was IDR1.5bn, a negligible return on book [S8, F67]. Book is a conservative mark: at attributable net assets the holdings would be worth about a twentieth of the target more, disclosed and not added. Read against the market, cash at face plus the associate at book means the market pays about a third of last year's EBITDA for the estate, just over two fifths after the related-party haircut; excluding the associate it is nine tenths of one year's EBITDA.

On asset value the estate is 110,982 planted hectares, 84,744 mature oil palm, and net fixed assets of IDR5,087.6bn is a small historical cost per hectare, so book is not a replacement mark [S6, F32, F40; S8, F61]. At the report price the FY2025 dividend yield of 5.3% is below the 11.2% cost of equity, so on its dividend the market prices a governance discount and a retained-cash story, not a yield; the earnings yield, the inverse of the 5.6x P/E, is not the binding comparator for a minority that cannot force distribution.

The cross-checks. EV/EBITDA uses the twenty-five-name peer median 5.7x and gives Rp3,436; the own-history leg is unusable because earlier years are distorted by impairment, so the blend falls back to the peer median [S0]. P/BV blends the peer median with an own average below book to 1.1x, giving Rp2,367. Both sit below the DCF, by a third and a half. The DCF-to-peer gap is a terminal-value effect, not a cash effect: EV is operating FCFF only, with cash and the associate added after it in the equity bridge, so the multiple holds no deposit yield. The terminal value is eight and a quarter times FY2035E EBITDA of IDR3,610.2bn against 5.7x peers, because an 11.2% cost of equity and two and a half per cent growth capitalise mature cash flow at a richer multiple than peers on trailing operating EV; at the peer multiple the terminal would cut the target about a tenth, rating unchanged.

The bridge has three items. The trapped-cash discount is charged only to the related-party cash at PT Bank Ina Perdana, IDR665.0bn at 30 September, 4.0% of assets and under a tenth of cash [S8, F53, F54]; in the persistence state it is worth about two fifths of face, so the even-odds charge is roughly three tenths of that slice. The announced IDR750.0bn buyback to 31 December 2026 [S9] is counted at half size and even odds. The third is a deduction, not an addition: a related-party deployment charge at a quarter probability, the probability-weighted cost of the group using the cash pile at twice fair value, which the investment-risks section sizes and justifies on the related-party share of revenue and the absence of a minority veto [S7, S13].

The other IDR7,629.3bn of third-party deposits is carried at face [S8, F57]. There is no precedent for a principal loss at unrelated banks in our archive, and the haircut is not a credit loss: it is the value of cash permanently undistributable to minorities. We apply it to the related-party slice and carry the whole-balance trap as the governance bear. Even odds stand both ways: the payout was cut and there is no minority veto, but every year has been paid and a buyback is running [S12, S9, S13].

Charging the whole balance at even odds instead of the slice lowers the target about a fifteenth. With the whole balance trapped at certainty the operating bear sits about a quarter above the price, so the governance state no longer loses money. The price implies something more extreme: a fourth CPO path at about half the deck, the reverse-DCF state at US$640/t against 1,240.0 USD/t [S0, S15], the only modelled state below the price. We judge it one chance in ten, because two years of flat dollar realisation and a persistent discount is what a market expecting sub-cycle prices looks like [S8, S3]. The published weights are base fifty, bear twenty-five, bull twenty-five and the target Rp4,689 is exactly that weighted value. Giving the fourth path its own one-in-ten weight and scaling the others to nine tenths gives about four thousand four hundred rupiah, some seven per cent below the published target — disclosed. The target sits about that far above our own distribution; the rating survives because even that blend is nearly three times the price.

One reading caveat applies to the grids. Both are struck from the base scenario inside the engine's sensitivity routine, before the scenario probabilities, so even the clean grid's centre prints at the base value of Rp4,618 and not at the published target of Rp4,689. The benchmark-and-rupiah grid is looser still: each override freezes its own driver after the explicit deck years, so its no-shock cell also prints below Rp4,618 and its cells are relative reads, not alternative targets. The benchmark override holds the benchmark at its last explicit level, so a multiplier of one changes nothing until FY2031E, where the average selling price stays at 893.5 USD/t instead of rising to 915.8 USD/t, and that freeze alone costs about a fifteenth of the base value. The rupiah override leaves the benchmark path identical and freezes IDR/USD instead, costing a little over a hundredth. The benchmark override is therefore the larger of the two, and the first year either override changes is FY2031E, not the first forecast year. The volume-and-cost grid touches no benchmark and its centre reproduces the base value exactly; its horizontal axis is a cost-intensity multiplier that carries the mining template's strip-ratio label but is pinned at one here. Read both for shape: both axes run close to one-for-one and symmetrically at the steps the table prints — a stronger rupiah takes about as much as a weaker one adds per step, and the near-a-fifth fall the earlier draft attributed to a stronger rupiah is the benchmark's widest step, not the rupiah's — because the benchmark revenue is dollar-referenced while most of the cost base is rupiah, and volume and cost intensity move the value only a few per cent per step [S0].

The price implies CPO of about US$640/t at the reference year, about half the deck's 1,240.0 USD/t on the same new-series deck [S0, S15]. Crediting cash near face and the associate at book, it implies about a third of last year's EBITDA for the estate. Either the market expects CPO at about half the deck for longer than we do, or it expects the cash to be consumed by the group.

The largest risk is that the discount is permanent. London Sumatra is a controlled subsidiary of a family group, most output is sold to its parent, and a material share of cash sits with a related bank — IDR665.0bn, 4.0% of total assets, withdrawable at the group's discretion [S8, F53]. Minorities cannot force a distribution, the payout has been cut once, and a value investor can be right about the asset and wrong about the exit for years. That is the value-trap configuration and we charge for it: the bridge carries a quarter probability on a value-destroying related-party deployment before FY2028 — two trillion rupiah at twice fair value destroys one trillion, about a thirty-second of the target — on top of the trapped-cash discount. The quarter is a judgement; the precedent is the related-party share of revenue and the absence of a minority veto [S7, F34, S13].

The second risk is CPO. The base uses the house deck, which embeds a near-term El Nino premium; if the weather fades and Malaysian stocks rebuild, price could fall by a quarter or more [S11]. The bear models that with a volume shortfall, a working-capital stretch and a real cost base three tenths above the last actual. The GAPKI warning cuts both ways: a 3m tonne loss meeting a B50 mandate that needs 14m tonnes is the bull's price case, while the same loss on London Sumatra's own estates is the bear's volume case [S24, S22]. A five per cent company-level shortfall takes roughly a twentieth off EBITDA and a ten per cent shortfall roughly a tenth, much less off the target because cash and the associate carry most of the value; only the fifteen per cent shortfall is run, as the bear.

The third cluster is operational and regulatory. Deferred fertiliser is a cost risk [S22]; the levy and biodiesel mandate change the domestic price [S10]; from January the reported single-channel export regime adds an unpublished intermediary cost between the group's refineries and the world market [S20, S21]; and GAPKI named policy stability itself as a risk [S24]. A one-to-five per cent pass-through into the related-party offtake, 63.3% of revenue, is about one and a half to eight per cent of EBITDA and moves the target one to four per cent, carried in the bear. A domestic levy at thirty to sixty dollars per tonne would take six to twelve per cent of FY2026E EBITDA as a one-year effect, and capitalised as a permanent cost five to nine per cent of the target; the bear carries forty dollars. None is existential for a debt-free producer.

Two downsides are sized: FY2024's IDR296.2bn rubber impairment could recur under the bear [S7]. Turnover of IDR17.8bn and a 40.4% public float clear the fund's floor, so no liquidity discount applies [S0, S13, F60].

The scenarios mirror the base shock for shock. The bear holds CPO at seventy-one and a half per cent of the deck at the reference year [S15], volume down about a sixth, the real cost base three tenths higher (including the levy and the single-channel pass-through) and working capital stretched; it charges the related-party cash discount at even odds, so it is an operating bear rather than a governance state. It still produces Rp2,555, about three fifths above the price: even at the cycle's realised low the market pays less than the estate alone is worth. The bull raises price by two fifths, volume about a sixth, releases working capital and holds costs a fifth below the last actual; the buyback is in the bridge and the payout step-up is not added. The probability-weighted target is Rp4,689. Signposts that would change our view: a sustained CPO break below the bear, a 2027 harvest where London Sumatra's own output falls with the national crop while price does not rise [S24], a related-party transfer of cash out below market value, another payout cut, a levy materially above forty dollars, or the buyback abandoned.

The controlling shareholder is PT Salim Ivomas Pratama of the Indofood Agri group, holding 59.5%, with Indofood Agri a further stake; the group controls just under three fifths and the public holds 40.4% of the 6,820 m shares [S13]. We use the company's table, not the Yahoo insider field of seventy per cent, which is impossible and unused [S0, S13]. We find no pledge disclosure, control contest or restatement; the board has group nominees and independent commissioners [S7, S8]. Related-party dealings are the central governance fact: sales of more than three fifths of revenue to the parent, FFB purchases from related estates, finance income on deposits at a related bank and group service companies all appear in the notes [S7]. Each is disclosed at market-referenced terms, and the audited realisation discount to the benchmark was stable across the two audited years; the lower 2026 tape is the domestic-reference effect [S7, S15]. It is still a structure in which the minority depends on the holder's goodwill, and the market prices that dependence. The auditor is KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, with an unmodified opinion [S7]; the company does not revalue plantations, so P/BV is a floor. The dividend record is the counterweight: a payout every year, thirty per cent for the last two years and thirty-five before [S12]. The cut is why the trap probability stays at even odds.

On ESG the exposures are land and deforestation, peat, labour and smallholder relations. The estates are long established, the company operates plasma partnerships and reports against the national sustainability standard [S6].

The near-term catalyst is the full-year result and the dividend declaration that follows. The interim showed profit up two fifths and cash higher, so the base for the final dividend is strong [S3, S8]. The buyback runs to 31 December 2026 on internal cash [S9]; execution at the current price is accretive because the shares trade below the cash they represent.

Policy is the third catalyst: the B50 mandate and monthly export levy reset determine the domestic CPO price and the group's offtake economics [S10], and a domestic levy is the risk we watch. On 1 January the reported DSI portal is due to open for CPO and coal, unconfirmed until the rule issues; we watch the published fee and whether the group's export netback moves [S20, S21].

The operational signposts are FFB output, extraction rate and external FFB purchases; nine months showed recovery on all three [S3], and a reversal would test the bear. GAPKI dates the heaviest El Nino impact to the 2027 harvest [S24, F68], so the first-half production report is where the warning shows up in London Sumatra's own yields or does not. Above all we monitor related-party flows: a change in the offtake, the deposit relationship or the group's willingness to let cash accumulate matters more than the CPO price [S7, S13].

valuation.label: P/BV
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: The discount persists and the cycle troughs at the same time. The related-party cash slice at Bank Ina Perdana of Rp665.016bn at 30-Sep-2026 is not withdrawn and the whole-balance governance failure is quoted as a separate state in section 5 [S8, F53]. On top of that, CPO is held at 71.5% of the new-series deck for the whole forecast, close to 29% below the deck own floor and stated only as a percentage of the current deck: the pre-2026 World Bank levels and averages are not comparable after the January-2026 series replacement [S15, p.3], so no cross-series level is used anywhere in this paper. The El Nino premium unwinds and Malaysian stocks rebuild [S11], a weaker FFB crop cuts volume 15% from the 300 kt plan - the GAPKI 3m tonne national loss [S24, F68] made company-specific, with a second season of fertiliser deferred on cost [S22] - and the parent receivable stretches working capital twofold from the FY2025 3.3% of revenue, which is the widest shock the engine bounds allow; the FY2024 actual stretch to 21.7% is disclosed in sections 3 and 5 as a stress beyond the kept scenario set, so the one year that actually stretched is representable even though the multiplier cannot reach it [S0, F34]. The cost stress is 30% above the FY2025 real level: 20% from external FFB and fertiliser, plus a USD40/t domestic CPO levy and a 2% pass-through of the DSI single-channel fee into the parent offtake, together about 8% of the cash cost. The domestic levy is the one policy that reaches a wholly domestic seller if the B50 funding need is met from domestic CPO; it is a bear risk, not a base assumption, because no domestic levy is in force in November 2026 [S10]. With the whole balance trapped at certainty instead of even odds this operating bear is worth Rp1,926, still above the current price: that is the governance-failure state, and it is quoted in section 5 rather than run as a fourth scenario because the bridge probability is a single model input shared by all scenarios.

bull.narrative: A severe El Nino and the B50 mandate lift CPO two fifths above the deck, as they did in the 2021-22 squeeze [S10, S11]: a 3m tonne loss of Indonesian supply in the 2027 harvest [S24, F68] meeting 14m tonnes of mandated biodiesel demand [S22, F69], a normal Q4, the maturing 6,054 ha of immature oil palm and a yield recovery from the weather-depressed base take volume 17.6% above the 300 kt plan; faster collection from SIMP releases working capital; and the extraction-rate and FFB-purchase programme hold the real cash cost a fifth below the FY2025 level [S3]. The announced Rp750bn buyback, running 26-Oct to 31-Dec-2026 on internal cash [S9], is carried as a probability-weighted partial in the valuation bridge, not as a scenario shock because its size is a ceiling. A step-up to the group sister's 50% payout is a board decision and is not added to the value: once the cash is credited at face, a higher payout distributes value already counted and is not an incremental asset; it matters only in the trapped state that the bear carries.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the 9M-2026 run-rate plus a normal Q4: CPO sales were 222 kt in the nine months (+7% yoy, [S3]) and Q4-2025 was 82.5 kt of the 290 kt year [F1], giving about 300 kt. Production supports it: 9M-2026 CPO output rose 12% to 227 kt on nucleus FFB up 7% to 850 kt [S3], and FY2025 production was 292 kt [F33]. The estate is mature and not expanding: nucleus oil palm is 90,798 ha with only 7% immature [F32], so the plan is held flat at 300 kt with no yield-growth assumption, inside the 15% drift gate. FY2025 sales of 290 kt are the last audited actual [F1]. Unchanged by the 12-Nov-2026 GAPKI warning that El Nino could cost Indonesian production up to 3m tonnes with the heaviest impact in the 2027 harvest [S24, F68]: that is an industry aggregate, not company guidance, and the chairman said the impact is already felt across industry players, including farmers who deferred fertiliser on cost, while London Sumatra's nucleus output was up 12% in the nine months to September [S24, S3]. The loss is national and industry-wide, not confined to smallholder estates [S24, S22]. A company-level cut on a national number would be the unsourced haircut the base-case rule forbids; the yield risk is carried in the bear at a 15% volume shortfall [S24]. The company sensitivity is disclosed in section 5: a 5% and a 10% shortfall on the 300 kt plan, each priced with the same margin and royalty mechanics as the base, so the reader can see what the GAPKI case costs if it reaches nucleus estates. Note the plan is already 1.5% below the 304.5 kt implied by 222 kt of nine-month sales plus the 82.5 kt Q4-2025 [S3, F47, F1]; holding the plan below that arithmetic is deliberate, because the nine-month number carries a +7% year on year against a weak 2025 base and the estate is not expanding [S3, F32].

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Recalibrated on the last actual, the 9M-2026 interim, and held flat. CPO (MKS) revenue of Rp3,342.357bn [S8, F48] over 222 kt of CPO sales [S3, F47] is Rp15.056m per tonne; at the model's FY2026E usd_idr of 17,570 [S0] that is USD 856.9/t against the deck's 9M-2026 average of USD 1,131/t (Q1 1,081, Q2 1,164, Q3 1,148, [S15]), a realisation of 0.758. The numerator and the denominator are on one series: the World Bank Pink Sheet states "October 2026: Replacement series for Palm oil from January 2026" [S15, p.3], and the house deck records that "the World Bank re-based the palm oil series from January 2026 ... so pre-2026 annual averages and the 2026 monthly tape are not perfectly homogeneous" [fund record]. The audited FY2025 ratio of 0.852 (Rp14.114m/t against the pre-replacement 1,007 series at 16,448.09 [F3]) is therefore not the like-for-like comparator and is not used: no published factor bridges the old and new series, and applying a 2026-series ratio to a 2025-series benchmark is the mismatch the red team identified. What is homogeneous in rupiah is the realised price against the domestic Harga Referensi/KPB: Rp14.114m/t in FY2025 against the Rp14,234/kg KPB average [F41, S6], or 0.992. The 9M-2026 realised rupiah price of Rp15.056m/t is +6.7% on FY2025 while the new-series dollar benchmark is +12.3%, and the rupiah is +6.8% weaker, so the company takes the domestic reference rather than the export print; that domestic-reference lag and the unquantified series break together explain why the model carries 0.758 and not 0.852. Holding 0.758 flat rather than fading it is the last-actual rule; the peer ratios near 0.78 are measured against other benchmarks and are not directly comparable. At the 30-Sep-2026 balance-sheet rate of Rp17,998 [S8] the same revenue/volume is USD 836.5/t, a 0.740 ratio, which brackets the estimate from below. The mechanism behind the wedge is named, not assumed: (i) the export levy and duty, which move monthly with the reference price and were cut by a fifth to USD 246.36/t for November from USD 308.27 in October, a per-tonne charge on the exported benchmark that no domestic sale bears [S10, F38]; and (ii) the domestic reference itself, the Harga Referensi/KPB, which is administratively set and averaged Rp14,234/kg in FY2025 against the realised Rp14.114m/t, a 0.992 rupiah ratio [S6, F41]. Because the levy is a per-tonne wedge that falls as the reference price falls, a constant dollar ratio is the neutral middle between two defensible anchors: at the audited old-series 0.852 the engine target is about a tenth above the base but it re-imports the pre-2026 benchmark; at USD 856.9/t held flat in nominal dollar terms for ten years the realisation ratio fades with the rising deck and the target falls a mid-single-digit percentage below base, because the domestic reference does not follow the export print. Taking the middle and saying so is the most probable path; the flat-dollar world is carried in the bear's cost and price stress, not the base.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no DMO-style domestic price cap applies to Indonesian CPO sales in this period; the B40/B50 mandate is a demand driver, not a cap on LSIP's selling price [S10].

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Palm oil cost intensity is expressed per tonne of CPO, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and all cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no overburden analogue in a plantation [S7].

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of CPO (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the last audited year and escalated with IDR inflation only. FY2025 COGS of Rp3,250.368bn [F7] less the Rp373.058bn of depreciation inside it [F30] leaves Rp2,877.310bn of cash cost for all products; the non-CPO cost of Rp617.854bn on Rp1,418.588bn of PK, rubber and other revenue at the 56.45% other margin [F28] is stripped out, leaving Rp2,259.456bn of CPO cash cost, or Rp7.791m per tonne on 290 kt [F1]. That is 21% above FY2024's Rp6.420m [F31] because external FFB purchases jumped to Rp672.332bn from Rp488.924bn [S7]; we hold the FY2025 level rather than extrapolate either year. The 2.5% annual escalation is the macro deck's long-run IDR inflation [S0], so the real cost base is flat and the FY2025 gross-margin gain is not assumed to repeat.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default scalar set to zero: the fuel driver is empty for PLANTATIONS, so the fuel term does not enter the cost build [S7].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: haulage, milling and port costs are already inside the per-tonne CPO cash cost backed out of the FY2025 LK [F30]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: 63.26% of revenue is sold domestically to SIMP [F34] and Indonesia's CPO export levy is borne by the exporter at shipment (USD 246.36/t, [F38]), not by LSIP on a domestic sale. The FY2025 cost-of-sales note carries no royalty or export-levy line [S7].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (PK, rubber, others)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-CPO revenue was Rp1,418.588bn: palm kernel and related products 1,093.304, rubber 149.982 and others 175.302 [F28]. It is escalated at 2.5% IDR inflation with flat volume, since PK output tracks CPO throughput and rubber prices move with the same cost base [S7, S0]; the FY2024 comparative of Rp921.664bn [F29] was lower because PK prices were weak, not because the product mix changed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: 56.45%: the FY2025 residual implies Rp617.854bn of cost on Rp1,418.588bn of non-CPO revenue once the CPO cash cost is set at Rp7.791m per tonne [F28]. PK and rubber are by-products of FFB already harvested for CPO, so the incremental cost is pressing, handling and freight only; the ratio is held flat.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A of Rp389.453bn (fixed assets 383.284, right-of-use 5.129, deferred charges 1.040, [F13]) over the 300 kt plan is Rp1.298m per tonne. The pack's Rp4.8bn D&A line is defective and has been replaced by the audited Note 25 charge [F13]. The 9M-2026 charge of Rp304.770bn (segment 292.398 plus unallocated 12.372, [S8]) annualises to about Rp406bn, so the FY2025 base is not stale. Escalated at 2.5% IDR; there is no revaluation uplift because LSIP does not apply the PSAK 16 revaluation model [S6].

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 additions to fixed assets were Rp433.312bn [F15], or 7.9% of revenue, spread across replanting, machinery, plasma and infrastructure (segment capex 393.856 plus unallocated 39.456, [S7]); over the 300 kt plan that is Rp1.444m per tonne. The 9M-2026 run-rate of Rp264.471bn [S8] supports the same intensity. Held in real terms with 2.5% IDR escalation rather than assuming a step-down after the current replanting push [S0].

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: LSIP's capex is volume-linked replanting, machinery and plasma support rather than discrete expansion projects, and the planted area has been flat-to-down (110,982 ha in 2025 vs 114,111 ha in 2021, [F32]); all of it is carried in capex_unit.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 3.3%, the FY2025 actual: operating working capital was Rp181.720bn or 3.3% of revenue in FY2025 [S0]. The FY2024 spike of 21.7% and FY2023's 7.3% [S0] are not extrapolated: the swing is the receivable from parent SIMP, 63.26% of revenue [F34], and the last actual is the right anchor. The working-capital caution is carried in the bear, which stretches the ratio 30%.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 17.2%, the FY2025 effective rate: income tax of Rp391.187bn [F24] on pre-tax profit of Rp2,277.542bn [F9]. Held flat; the 22% headline is reduced by the permanent differences on plasma and land income that recur in the LK [S7].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8% on a negligible balance: FY2025 finance costs were Rp1.176bn [F23] against lease liabilities of under Rp1bn, and the group carries no bank borrowings at 30-Sep-2026 [F37]. The rate is set so a future lease or drawdown prices sensibly rather than at the engine's 15% clamp.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4.6%, the three-year average of finance income over opening cash: 5.06% in FY2025 (Rp276.021bn [F21] on Rp5,453.691bn), 4.81% in FY2024 and 4.04% in FY2023 [S0]. The balance is held largely on deposit and partly at related-party Bank Ina Perdana, which supplied Rp44.005bn of FY2025 finance income [S7].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the group has no interest-bearing bank debt at 30-Sep-2026, only lease liabilities [F37, S8], and capex plus the dividend are covered by operating cash flow of Rp3,015.733bn in FY2025 [S7]. The announced Rp750bn buyback [S9] is assumed to be funded from cash, not debt.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating income or charge is disclosed beyond the associate line (a Rp5.691bn loss in FY2025) and that is immaterial against EBITDA [S7].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: non-controlling interests are Rp3.833bn of a Rp13,999.946bn equity base and their share of profit was a Rp1.401bn loss in FY2025 [S7], so the minority line is immaterial.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 30%: the company declares 30% of profit, DPS Rp83 for FY2025 and Rp65 for FY2024 on 6,819,963,965 shares [F18, S12]. The FY2025 cash payment of Rp443.234bn was the FY2024 dividend [F17]; the 30% policy is held rather than the engine's default.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: shares outstanding are 6,819,963,965 and unchanged across the audited years [F20]. The Rp750bn buyback announced in October 2026 [S9] is not yet executed and its size is a ceiling, so it is treated as upside in section 5 rather than modelled as a completed reduction.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5% nominal IDR, the macro deck's long-run inflation [S0]. With volume flat and CPO prices and costs both escalating at about inflation, real FCFF is flat; a 4% terminal rate would add real growth the business has not shown (nucleus FFB has been flat at 1.34-1.38m tonnes since 2021, [S6]).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue (cash)
assumptions.basis: 4.6%, the FY2025 net operating cost ratio implied by the filing: gross profit Rp2,261.338bn less operating profit Rp2,008.388bn = Rp252.950bn of net operating cost on Rp5,511.706bn of revenue [F11]. It nets other operating income (Rp136.905bn of FX, land-usage and PK-shell income) against selling (Rp73.099bn) and G&A (Rp247.878bn) and the Rp59.571bn bio-asset fair-value loss [S7]. FY2024's 9.7% is not the run-rate because it carries the Rp296.164bn one-off impairment [F12]. Held flat, so no drift.

challenges.challenge: The new caveat says the rupiah axis is asymmetric, a weaker rupiah adding about a tenth of value at a tenth of move and a stronger one taking nearly a fifth. The grid does not show that: at benchmark x1.0 the FX column runs 3,858.22 at 0.9 and 4,648.93 at 1.1 around 4,253.58, so each direction is 9.3 pct per 10 pct. The nearly-a-fifth figure is the response to a 20 pct move (FX 0.8 gives 3,703.62 against a base of 4,618.30). The two clauses measure different move sizes and the claimed asymmetry is absent at the steps the table prints.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Re-ran the grid: at benchmark x1.0 the rupiah column runs 3,858.22 at 0.9 and 4,648.93 at 1.1 around 4,253.58, so both directions are about 9.3 pct per step. Dropped the asymmetry claim, said both axes run near one-for-one, and attributed the near-a-fifth fall to the benchmark widest step, not the rupiah [S0].

challenges.challenge: The caveat attributes one mechanism to both axes: any override, the rupiah axis as much as the benchmark axis, re-prices the whole benchmark path from the first forecast year and drops the post-explicit escalation. An FX-only override at x1.0 leaves the benchmark ASP path identical (917.18, 894.44, 893.49 for FY2028E to FY2030E) and freezes the IDR/USD path instead, costing 1.4 pct; a benchmark override at x1.0 changes nothing until FY2031E (ASP frozen at 893.49 against 915.83) and costs 6.7 pct. The sentence names the wrong driver for the FX axis and the wrong start year for both.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Single-driver what-ifs confirm the red team: benchmark x1.0 freezes the benchmark at 1,178.75 and the ASP at 893.49 from FY2031E, costing 6.7 pct; FX x1.0 leaves the benchmark path identical, freezes IDR/USD and costs 1.4 pct. The caveat now says each override freezes its own driver, the benchmark override is the larger, and FY2031E is the first affected year [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the bridge has two items and describes only the trapped-cash discount and the buyback. valuation.bridge carries three: the third is the related-party deployment charge of minus 1,000bn at 0.25 probability, minus 250bn expected or about Rp37 per share, which section 5 says the bridge carries. A reader cannot reconcile target to bridge from section 4.
challenges.answer: Accepted. valuation.bridge carries three items, not two; added the related-party deployment charge at a quarter probability in a single clause and pointed the reader to the investment-risks section where its sizing and the related-party evidence for the probability are set out [S7, S13, S8].

challenges.challenge: The asset-value paragraph cites no source id although it carries five load-bearing numbers (110,982 planted ha, 84,744 mature ha, 5,087.6bn net fixed assets) and a yield comparison. The 5.3 pct it sets against the 11.2 pct cost of equity is the FY2025 dividend yield at the report price (DPS 83 over 1,560), an odd comparator for a required return when the earnings yield is 17.7 pct.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added [S6, F32, F40; S8, F61] to the asset-value paragraph and labelled the 5.3 pct as the FY2025 dividend yield, adding that the earnings yield implied by the P/E is not the binding comparator for a minority that cannot force distribution [S6, S8].

missing_bull_case.note: Carried from the published round, not re-litigated: no modelled state narrows the 0.68x P/BV discount. The edit adds no new bull-side error and now discloses the associate at attributable NAV, about a twentieth of target.

missing_bear_case.note: For this refresh: section 4 discloses the one-in-ten sub-cycle CPO path at about 4,400, below the 4,689 target, and the whole-balance-trapped variant. The deployment charge is in the model and section 5; the section 4 prose omits it, filed as C3.

assumption_realism.note: No assumption edited: fund record and fund record are untouched and model inputs are identical to the v4 run. Volume, realisation, cost, royalty, payout and tax all as published.

evidence_and_citations.note: Spot-checked in archive: cash 8,516.274 and third-party deposits 7,629.349 and Bank Ina 665.016 at 3.97 pct [S8], buyback 750bn to 31-Dec-2026 [S9], levy 246.36 [S10], SIMP 59.51 pct [S13], planted 110,982 ha [S6], series break [S15 p.3]. The section 4 asset-value paragraph carries no source id, filed as C4.

valuation_method_fit.note: Grids reconciled cell by cell to the engine: volume-and-cost centre 4,618.2976 equals tp_base exactly; benchmark-and-FX centre 4,253.575 is 7.9 pct below, about 6.7 pct from the benchmark override and 1.4 pct from the FX one. The caveat explains the first correctly and the second wrongly, filed as C2.

bias_and_tone.note: The report still discloses that the target sits about 7 pct above its own one-in-ten-weighted distribution and that the price implies a sub-cycle CPO path. The caveat adds caution rather than removing it; its error overstates downside, not upside.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck wiring unchanged: d.agri.cpo in USD/t, IDR cost currency, unit_factor 0.001, royalty flat at zero on domestic sales, g 2.5 pct. Both grid axes read the same deck variables as the model.

conservatism_audit.note: Carried from the published round: volume 300 against a 304.5 kt run-rate, capex flat at 433.3 nominal while costs escalate, D&A 1.298m per tonne against 1.356m annualised. The refresh changes none of them and adds no haircut, so no new challenge is filed.

calibration.note: Engine qc blocking empty; the minus 10.4 pct calibration gap stays justified and I re-verified the quoted sentence in S15 p.3. Re-running the engine moved tp 0.016 pct (4,688.43 to 4,689.16) on the stub asof; the published Rp4,689 is unchanged.

signoff.notes: Approved as it now stands. C1-C4 all answered on substance and the rewritten S4 matches the engine: each override freezes its own driver, the benchmark x1.0 freeze costs 6.7 pct and the rupiah one 1.4 pct, first affected year FY2031E; the bridge now says three items including the -1,000bn x 0.25 deployment charge; the asset paragraph is sourced [S6, F32, F40; S8, F61] and the 5.3 pct is labelled the dividend yield. QC Q1 (FIX) accepted as immaterial to the published text: the engine's whole-balance-at-certainty bear is Rp1,887 = +21.0 pct against the price, so 'about a quarter' overstates that cushion by about four points and nothing else; no rating, target or input depends on it, the qualitative point that the governance state sits above the price stands, and the phrase should read 'about a fifth' at the next touch. QC Q2 (FIX) accepted: the two stale numbers live only in assumptions qc_justifications (DCF EV 24,706.5 vs 24,713.7; FY2025 DPS yield 5.5 vs 5.3 pct), neither appears in published text nor feeds an input, and QC itself marked it for the next version. Lint warning of 3,840 words against the 3,500 refresh range noted as cosmetic. Bias: single-name sign-off batch; comps show LSIP COE/WACC 11.18 pct and g 2.5 pct in line with AALI 11.18 pct and 2.5 pct, and the peer set is mixed (four BUY, two SELL), so no shared-input tilt. Calibration: the -10.4 pct gate gap is the World Bank palm series break (FY2025A 1,007 old series vs 2026 1,131 new series) plus the flat domestic reference; the 0.758 realisation reproduces the 9M-2026 actual 856.9 USD/t and the FY2025 audited 858.1, so no default haircut and no understatement carried into FY+1. Target arithmetic reconciles: 5,044 at 60 pct, 3,436 at 25, 2,367 at 15 blend to 4,240, times 1.1118 less 96 gives 4,618, and the 50/25/25 scenarios give 4,689. Sources are filings, news, World Bank, Damodaran and company IR; no broker research, ratings, targets or consensus met, so no contamination.

bias.note: Base case sits on the last actual: FY2026E ASP 860.3 USD/t reproduces the 9M-2026 realised 856.9 [S8,F48,S3,F47] and the FY2025 audited 858.1 [F3]; costs are the FY2025 cash cost 7,791,431 Rp/t escalated at 2.5% IDR only; D&A 1.298m/t, tax 17.2%, payout 30% and NWC 3.3% are all the last actual [F13,F24,F18]; volume 300 kt is 1.5% BELOW the 304.5 kt 9M-plus-Q4 arithmetic [S3,F47,F1], the one departure from the plan and it is downward and sourced. No driver is above the company plan except the deck's own FY2027E 1,240 [S15]. Scenarios mirrored on the same four drivers (CPO 0.715/1.399, volume 0.85/1.176, NWC 2.0/0.5) with base at 50%; the only asymmetry is cost 1.3x bear vs 0.8x bull (reciprocal 0.77), which leans bearish, not bullish.

findings.finding: S4 says the whole-balance-trapped-at-certainty bear 'sits about a quarter above the price'. Engine with the whole Rp8,516.274bn balance at 58.9% at certainty gives bear tp Rp1,887 vs price Rp1,560 = +21.0%, i.e. about a fifth, and the bear DCF falls to Rp1,141 (-27%) because only the primary method is struck on it.

Two stale numbers in assumptions qc_justifications: dcf_multiple quotes DCF EV Rp24,706.5bn where the current run and S4 both say Rp24,713.7bn; extreme_call quotes the FY2025 DPS yield at 5.5% where Rp83/Rp1,560 is 5.3% (as S4 states). Neither moves the call.
S3 cites [S10, F41] for the Rp14,234/kg domestic KPB, but F41's source is S6 (annual report); S10 is the export-levy article and carries no KPB.

The lower 2026 realisation ratio is explained in S3/S4 as the World Bank series replacement [S15 p.3] but in S6 as 'the domestic-reference effect'. Both are defensible but only one mechanism should be named.

Cost-intensity shock is not exactly mirrored: bear 1.3x vs bull 0.8x (reciprocal 0.769), so the bull is ~3pp less generous than the bear is harsh. Direction is bearish, so it does not inflate the target.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 2,148.3 vs the actual 2,397.8 (-10%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: The -10.4% gap is a series break in the denominator plus a domestic-reference lag in the numerator, and the gate is not a like-for-like test. S15 p.3 states "October 2026: Replacement series for Palm oil from January 2026", and fund record states "the World Bank re-based the palm oil series from January 2026 ... so pre-2026 annual averages and the 2026 monthly tape are not perfectly homogeneous" [S15]. The 0.758 realisation is fitted inside the 2026 new series: 9M-2026 CPO revenue of Rp3,342.357bn over 222 kt is Rp15.056m/t, or USD 856.9/t at 17,570, against the new-series 9M-2026 average of USD 1,131/t [S8, S3, S15]. The gate then applies that 2026-series ratio to the pre-replacement FY2025A benchmark of 1,007 USD/t, giving USD 763.3/t against the FY2025 actual of USD 858.1/t. No published factor bridges the two series, so the gap cannot be closed by calibration; the audited 0.852 belongs to the old series and is not imported into the new-series forecast. The second component is real: LSIP sells at the domestic Harga Referensi/KPB, which averaged Rp14,234/kg in FY2025 [F41] against a realised Rp14.114m/t, 0.992 in rupiah, while CIF Rotterdam rose 15% that year [S6]; in 9M-2026 the realised rupiah price rose 6.7% while the new-series dollar benchmark rose 12.3% and the rupiah weakened 6.8%, so the dollar realisation fell. On the comparison the gate is trying to make, the FY2026E model ASP of USD 860.3/t at the FY2026E benchmark of 1,135 USD/t is flat against FY2025's USD 858.1/t [S0, S7]. For disclosure, the engine target at the peer-median realisation of 0.780 is Rp4,849 and at the audited old-series 0.852 is Rp5,268, both above the base target only because 0.852 re-imports the old, lower benchmark; neither is the base case.

flags.message: opex FY2024A restated at 6.02x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's FY2024 opex of Rp73.251bn is not an opex line: it is gross profit less a pack EBIT that was itself computed as gross profit minus that number, with the biological-asset fair-value gain, other operating income and other operating expenses all left out. The audited FY2024 statement carries selling of Rp48.267bn, G&A of Rp239.897bn, other operating income of Rp142.225bn and other operating expenses of Rp437.610bn, which includes the Rp296.164bn impairment in the others segment [S7]; gross profit of Rp1,991.961bn less operating profit of Rp1,550.851bn is Rp441.110bn, 6.02x the pack. FY2024 is therefore keyed to the audited net operating cost, not to the pack residual [F12].

flags.message: expected return +207%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers. First, the balance sheet: cash of Rp8,516.274bn at 30-Sep-2026 with zero interest-bearing debt [F37] is 80% of the Rp10,639bn market capitalisation at the report price. Charging only the related-party slice with the probability-weighted trapped-cash haircut (Rp195.85bn), deducting the Rp1,261.143bn associate line [S8] but no other asset, the market is paying about Rp862bn at face cash, or 0.36x FY2025A EBITDA of Rp2,397.841bn, for an estate that earned that EBITDA in FY2025A [S7]; with the related-party haircut charged the estate is 0.44x, and excluding the associate line entirely it is 0.89x. Second, the cash return: DPS of Rp83 for FY2025 at a 30% payout [F18, S12] is a 5.5% yield at the current price, and a Rp750bn buyback runs from 26-Oct to 31-Dec-2026 on internal cash [S9]. Third, the reverse DCF: the price implies a CPO price of about USD 640.1/t against the FY2027E deck of USD 1,240/t, a 48% discount [S0, S15], on one new-series deck, and we quote no old-series level from the pre-2026 WB series. The target is the arithmetic of a 0.6-weight DCF at an 11.18% COE and 2.5% terminal growth, a config blend multiple on the two cross-checks, after the probability-weighted trapped-cash haircut on the related-party slice and the buyback bridge item; the risk that the discount persists is the core of section 5, not a modelling error.

news.title: DSI Jadi Perantara Tunggal Ekspor Sawit, Bagaimana Dampaknya terhadap Industri CPO RI?
news.note: PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia is planned as sole intermediary for commodity exports including crude palm oil; report examines impact on Indonesia's CPO industry.

news.title: Mulai 1 Januari 2027, Ekspor Sawit Wajib Lewat Platform DSI, Biaya Layanan Satu Digit Dolar AS
news.note: From 1 January 2027 all palm oil and derivative exports must go through the DSI platform, with a single-digit US dollar service fee.

news.note: GAPKI warned El Nino could cut national palm oil output by up to 3 million tonnes in 2027, a supply risk for listed CPO producers.

news.note: GAPKI chairman Eddy Martono said El Nino drought and fires could cut Indonesian palm output by up to 3 million tonnes and asked government to keep policy stable.

news.note: GAPKI warned that Indonesian palm output growth faces structural constraints from limited fertiliser use and slow replanting by smallholders, speaking at its Nusa Dua conference.
